content: A perfect gas is defined as a gas in which intermolecular forces are completely neglected. This means that, in addition to the assumptions made for an ideal gas, the following specific assumption is added: Neglected intermolecular forces: By disregarding these forces, the equation of state for a perfect gas can be derived directly from kinetic theory or statistical mechanics. This assumption simplifies calculations significantly, allowing the ideal gas law to be applied without any restrictions. It also eliminates the need to account for complications arising from intermolecular forces, such as Van der Waals forces. In addition to the definition of a perfect gas, there are two further simplifications that can be made. These are often omitted or combined into a general definition of a perfect gas in various textbooks. However, for clarity, these simplifications are defined separately: Thermally Perfect Gas The gas is assumed to be in thermodynamic equilibrium. The gas is not undergoing any chemical reactions. The internal energy, enthalpy, and specific heat capacities of the gas are considered to be functions of temperature only. Mathematically, this is expressed as: For example, it is applicable in modeling an axial compressor, where temperature variations are relatively small. In this model, heat capacity is allowed to vary, but only as a function of temperature. Additionally, molecular dissociation is not permitted. Calorically Perfect Gas The most restrictive gas model is the calorically perfect gas, which incorporates all the assumptions of a thermally perfect gas and adds the following condition: Constant specific heats: In this model, the specific heats (( C_v ) and ( C_p )) are assumed to remain constant. The relationships for internal energy and enthalpy are simplified further: ( e = C_v T ) (internal energy is directly proportional to temperature) ( h = C_p T ) (enthalpy is directly proportional to temperature) Although this is the most restrictive model, it can still provide sufficiently accurate results for many practical calculations. For instance, if one were to model a single compression stage of an axial compressor using both a variable ( C_p ) model and a constant ( C_p ) model, the deviation between the two results might be so small that other factors—such as compressor tip-clearance, boundary layer or frictional losses, and manufacturing imperfections—would have a greater impact on the final outcome than the assumption of constant ( C_p ).
